BAR-001.statement: A signed-in person can publish a chirp of 280 characters or fewer, attributed to their handle; an empty or over-limit message is refused and no chirp is created.

BAR-002.statement: A signed-in person's home timeline returns their own chirps and those of the people they follow, newest first, in bounded pages reached by a cursor — never the entire history in one response.

BAR-003.statement: A reply records the chirp it answers; a reply to a chirp that no longer exists is reported as not-found rather than accepted as though it succeeded.

BAR-004.statement: Liking a chirp increases its like count by one; liking it again does not increase the count further; unliking returns the count — the like is idempotent and the displayed count matches the result.

BAR-005.statement: Following a user brings that user's new chirps into the follower's timeline and is idempotent; unfollowing removes them; a person cannot follow their own account.

BAR-006.statement: A user's public profile — handle, display name, bio, and follower/following counts — is viewable with no session.
BAR-006.proposed: usable_early --- ## Real accounts and owner-only identity
BAR-006.final: usable_early --- ## Real accounts and owner-only identity

BAR-007.statement: Sign-up establishes a secret the person later uses to prove the account is theirs; an account created at sign-up cannot be entered by knowledge of its handle alone.

BAR-008.statement: Sign-up enforces handle format (up to 15 letters, digits, or underscores) and uniqueness, reporting a taken handle as a conflict naming it and an ill-formed handle as a field-level error; a valid, unused handle is accepted.

BAR-009.statement: Presenting only another account's handle, without its credential, grants no session; the legitimate owner presenting the credential set at sign-up or recovery is signed in.

BAR-010.statement: A sign-in attempt lets the person tell "no such account" from "credential did not match" — enough to distinguish a typo from a wrong secret — without revealing which accounts exist beyond what the product already makes public.

BAR-011.statement: Signed in as one account, every attempt through the product's surfaces to act as another account — post, reply, like, or follow as them, edit their profile or settings, or delete their content — is refused.

BAR-012.statement: A person's contact, credential, and session data are never returned to another user or in any public response; only the public fields (handle, display name, bio, public chirps, counts) are exposed.
BAR-012.proposed: usable_early --- ## Durability — what a person creates is still there
BAR-012.final: usable_early --- ## Durability — what a person creates is still there

BAR-013.statement: After the service is restarted, updated, or redeployed, an account created beforehand still exists and its chirps, follows, and likes are still present on the next sign-in. The in-memory store at `c805525`, which loses everything on restart, does not meet this.
BAR-013.proposed: usable_early --- ## The rest of the account lifecycle
BAR-013.final: usable_early --- ## The rest of the account lifecycle

BAR-014.statement: An account has a point of contact that the product confirms the person controls (a verification step) before it is relied on for recovery or important notices; the contact is kept minimal.

BAR-015.statement: A person who has lost their credential can regain access themselves by proving control of the verified contact, with no one acting on their behalf; a person without that verified contact cannot recover the account.

BAR-016.statement: After a person signs out, the session that was in use can no longer be used — replaying the prior request with it is rejected — so the next person at a shared device is not signed in as them.

BAR-017.statement: A signed-in person can change their display name and bio, and the change persists and shows on their profile on the next view.

BAR-018.statement: A signed-in person has a settings surface where they can view and update their verified contact and view and end their active sessions or devices.

BAR-019.statement: A signed-in person can obtain their own data — their chirps, profile, and follow list — in a portable form they can open and read outside chirp.

BAR-020.statement: A signed-in person can delete their own account; afterward the account can no longer sign in and the person's content is removed per the stated deletion outcome.

BAR-021.statement: The product states a definite outcome for deletion — what becomes of the person's chirps that others replied to or liked, and whether the freed handle can be re-registered — and its behavior after a deletion matches that stated outcome.

BAR-022.statement: Deletion is confirmed before it happens and explains what will and will not survive — including that export is the person's chance to keep a copy; cancelling at the confirmation deletes nothing.
BAR-022.proposed: releasable --- ## Safety, moderation, and operator support
BAR-022.final: releasable --- ## Safety, moderation, and operator support

BAR-023.statement: A signed-in person can report a chirp and report an account, and each submission is acknowledged as received.

BAR-024.statement: The product states the rules — what is and is not allowed — within the product, and a report can point to them.

BAR-025.statement: Through a supported interface, the operator can assist a user's recovery, remove a named chirp, and disable or action an abusive account, none of which requires editing stored data by hand.

BAR-026.statement: A visitor arriving with no account and no session sees an explanation of what chirp is and a clear path to sign up, rather than being stopped at a sign-in wall.

BAR-027.statement: Immediately after sign-up, with no follows and no posts, the person sees guidance explaining the empty state and at least one actionable way toward a non-empty timeline, not a blank page.

BAR-028.statement: An empty list, a loading list, and a failed action each present a state the person can understand and act on, rather than a blank area or a silent failure.

BAR-029.statement: An expired or invalid session routes the person to sign-in with their place explained rather than failing silently; a transient server error while posting can be recovered by retry without losing the drafted chirp.

BAR-030.statement: On a typical phone viewport, a person can read the timeline, compose and post, reply, like, follow, and view a profile with no broken layout or unreachable controls.

BAR-031.statement: Using keyboard navigation and a screen reader, a person can complete the core loop (read the timeline, compose and post, reply, like, follow, view a profile), and the controls expose accessible names and roles, to the baseline the experience design sets.
BAR-031.proposed: releasable --- ## Operational readiness to be a live service
BAR-031.final: releasable --- ## Operational readiness to be a live service

BAR-032.statement: An operator can produce a backup of user data and restore from it, bringing back accounts, chirps, and follows.

BAR-033.statement: The health/readiness signal reports not-ready when the product cannot actually serve users (for example its durable store is unavailable) and ready when it can — it means "serving users," not merely "the process is running."

BAR-034.statement: Over a sustained period the product responds at its address with the core loop working; unavailability is the exception, measured against the availability target the operational-readiness design sets.

BAR-035.statement: Posting or requesting beyond a reasonable rate is throttled or rejected rather than served without limit, so one actor cannot trivially overwhelm the service or flood others.

BAR-100.title: A registered person has exactly one account with the public profile fields
BAR-100.statement: Registering a person yields exactly one account carrying an opaque id, a handle, a display name, an optional bio (absent and empty-string are distinguishable), a creation time, and follower/following counts; no second "profile" entity exists, and that single entity is both the public profile others see and the account its holder manages.

BAR-101.title: Handles are well-formed and unique
BAR-101.statement: A handle of 1–15 characters, each an ASCII letter, digit, or underscore, is accepted; an empty, over-length, or otherwise invalid handle is refused against the handle field; and registering a handle already in use is refused as a conflict, so at most one account holds any handle.

BAR-102.title: Entity ids are opaque and server-assigned
BAR-102.statement: Account ids and chirp ids are assigned by the product and are opaque to clients; no create surface accepts a client-supplied id, and a client only echoes back an id the product issued.

BAR-103.title: An assigned id is never reused
BAR-103.statement: Once assigned to an entity, an account id or chirp id is never later observed on a different entity, including after the original entity is deleted.

BAR-104.title: Creation times are UTC, immutable, and totally ordered
BAR-104.statement: Every account and chirp carries a creation time in UTC epoch-milliseconds that does not change after creation, and two entities created in sequence carry times whose order matches the order they were created, so timestamps are directly comparable for ordering such as the newest-first timeline.

BAR-105.title: Profile edits apply; id and creation time do not change
BAR-105.statement: A signed-in holder can change their display name and bio and see the change on the next view, and no product surface ever changes an account's id or creation time.

BAR-106.title: A chirp is a bounded post with one existing author, immutable once posted
BAR-106.statement: Posting a chirp of 1–280 characters (counted by Unicode scalar value) attributed to the signed-in account yields a chirp carrying an id, that author, the body as written, a creation time, a like count of zero, and no reply target; an empty or over-length body is refused and no chirp is created; and after posting, the chirp's body and author never change.

BAR-107.title: A reply records an existing target chirp
BAR-107.statement: A reply records the id of exactly one chirp that exists at reply time; replying to a chirp id that does not exist or has been removed is refused as not-found, and no reply is created with a dangling target.

BAR-108.title: Following is directed, self-free, idempotent, and reversible
BAR-108.statement: A follow is recorded in one direction from one existing account to another; following one's own account is refused; following an account already followed changes nothing and does not duplicate the edge or double a count; and unfollowing removes the edge so the followee's chirps no longer enter the follower's timeline (unfollowing an account not followed changes nothing).

BAR-109.title: Follower and following counts equal the edges
BAR-109.statement: An account's follower count equals the number of accounts currently following it and its following count equals the number it currently follows; one follow raises the count by exactly one and an unfollow returns it.

BAR-110.title: A like is at most one per account and chirp, and the like count equals the likes
BAR-110.statement: Liking a chirp records one like from the account to that existing chirp; liking a chirp already liked changes nothing and does not add a second like; unliking removes it; and the chirp's like count equals the number of distinct accounts that currently like it, moving by exactly one on a like or unlike.

BAR-111.title: The home timeline is the derived, newest-first, paged view of self plus followed accounts
BAR-111.statement: A viewer's home timeline contains the viewer's own chirps and the chirps of every account the viewer currently follows and no others; it is ordered newest-first; it is returned a bounded page at a time with an opaque continuation cursor when more remain (a client cannot force every chirp into one response); and because it is derived, following or unfollowing an account changes what the next read returns with no stale materialized timeline.

BAR-112.title: A session authenticates as exactly one account and is carried as an opaque token
BAR-112.statement: A session authenticates requests as exactly one account, and every action taken under it is attributed to that account and no other; the session is presented as an opaque bearer token whose internal structure no client surface interprets.

BAR-113.title: A session can be ended and does not live forever
BAR-113.statement: A signed-in person can end their session (sign out) after which a request carrying that session's token is refused, and a session presented after its bounded lifetime has elapsed is refused and the person is returned to sign-in. Sign-out that invalidates the session is a release surface the product does not provide at `c805525`.

BAR-114.title: An account has an authentication credential distinct from its handle
BAR-114.statement: Each account has an associated authentication credential the holder proves themselves with, distinct from the handle, so that knowing only an account's handle never establishes a session for it; the credential value is never returned in any profile or public response.

BAR-115.title: An account has a verified point of contact for recovery
BAR-115.statement: Each account has an associated point of contact the product treats as verified before relying on it for account recovery; that contact value is never returned to another account or in a public response. A verified contact and the recovery it supports are a release surface the product does not provide at `c805525`.

BAR-116.title: Private account data is never exposed to others
BAR-116.statement: An account's credential, verified contact, and session data never appear in any public response or in another account's view; a profile fetched with no session or with a different account's session returns only the handle, display name, bio, follower/following counts, and public chirps.
BAR-116.proposed: usable_early ### Integrity, deletion, and a person's own data
BAR-116.final: usable_early ### Integrity, deletion, and a person's own data

BAR-117.title: Every reference resolves; no dangling reference is observable
BAR-117.statement: Through every product surface that creates a relationship, a chirp's author, a reply's target, a follow's two endpoints, and a like's account and chirp all name entities that exist or the action is refused; no surface produces a chirp, follow, reply, or like that names a nonexistent entity.

BAR-118.title: Account deletion has a single defined, applied outcome with no dangling reference
BAR-118.statement: The product states a single deletion outcome — what becomes of the account's chirps (including those others replied to or liked), its follow edges, and its likes, and whether its freed handle may be re-registered — and deleting an account applies exactly that outcome: the account can no longer sign in, the product's state matches the stated outcome, and no remaining entity references the deleted account in a way the outcome did not define. Account deletion is a release surface the product does not provide at `c805525`.

BAR-119.title: A person can obtain their own data in a portable form
BAR-119.statement: A signed-in person can obtain their own data — their profile, the full set of their chirps, and the full set of accounts they follow — because that data is enumerable per account. A self-service export is a release surface the product does not provide at `c805525`.

BAR-120.title: Server-maintained counts are never accepted as client input
BAR-120.statement: An account's follower and following counts and a chirp's like count are maintained by the product and are never honored as client input; a create or update request carrying such a count has no effect on the stored value.
BAR-120.proposed: usable_early ### Persistence — what must survive a restart (the durability gate)
BAR-120.final: usable_early ### Persistence — what must survive a restart (the durability gate)

BAR-130.title: The product's user state survives restart, update, and redeploy
BAR-130.statement: On a running deployment, an account created with chirps, follows, and likes is still present and unchanged — account, chirps, follows, likes, and active session — after the serving process is restarted and, separately, after it is redeployed; a person's content is intact on their next visit. This closes the `c805525` release blocker: the in-memory store loses everything on restart.

BAR-131.title: Accounts persist in full across a restart
BAR-131.statement: After a restart, an account reads back with the same id, handle, display name, bio (preserved as given, absent or present), and creation time, and its follower/following counts are unchanged; an account registered with no bio still reads back with its bio absent rather than an empty string.

BAR-132.title: Account private identity data persists durably and stays non-public across a restart
BAR-132.statement: An account's credential and verified contact persist across a restart so the holder can still sign in and still recover their account afterward, and that data never appears in any public response before or after the restart.

BAR-133.title: Chirps persist in full across a restart
BAR-133.statement: After a restart, each chirp reads back with the same id, author, body text, and creation time; a reply still records the id of the chirp it answers; and like counts are unchanged.

BAR-134.title: The follow graph persists across a restart
BAR-134.statement: After a restart, every follow edge is still recorded in the same direction, the followee's chirps still enter the follower's timeline, and both accounts' follower/following counts are unchanged.

BAR-135.title: Likes persist across a restart
BAR-135.statement: After a restart, each like is still recorded from the same account to the same chirp and the chirp's like count is unchanged.

BAR-136.title: Active sessions survive a restart; ended sessions stay ended
BAR-136.statement: A session obtained before a restart is still accepted afterward and still acts as the same account, so a redeploy does not silently sign a person out; a session that was ended (signed out) or has passed its lifetime is refused after a restart and is never revived by one.

BAR-137.title: Server-maintained counts are correct after a restart
BAR-137.statement: After a restart, each account's follower and following counts equal its current follow edges and each chirp's like count equals the distinct accounts that currently like it; a follow or like added or removed after the restart moves the relevant count by exactly one.

BAR-138.title: The timeline is reconstructable from durable data after a restart
BAR-138.statement: A timeline noted before a restart returns the same chirps in the same newest-first order after the restart with no further writes, reconstructed from the durable chirps and the durable follow graph; no separately stored timeline is required.
BAR-138.proposed: releasable ### Persistence — durability as a correctness property

BAR-139.title: An acknowledged write is durable before it is acknowledged
BAR-139.statement: A write the product confirms to a person — posting a chirp, following or unfollowing, liking or unliking, editing a profile, deleting an account — is present after a restart that occurs immediately after the acknowledgement, with no further action in between.

BAR-140.title: Referential integrity holds across restart and restore
BAR-140.statement: After a restart and, separately, after a restore from backup, traversing chirps, replies, follows, and likes resolves every referenced account and chirp; no stopping, restarting, or recovering of the product introduces a reference to an entity that is absent.

BAR-141.title: Ids stay unique and are never reused across a restart
BAR-141.statement: After a restart, ids already issued are never reassigned to a different entity and id generation does not reset to a point that collides with existing ids; accounts and chirps created after the restart carry ids that collide with none recorded before it, and no existing entity's id has changed.

BAR-142.title: An applied account deletion is durable and never half-applied
BAR-142.statement: Once applied, an account deletion's stated outcome survives a restart (the account still cannot sign in, the stated outcome still holds, the freed-handle policy still holds), and a restart during a deletion leaves the product with the deletion either fully applied or not applied — never a partially deleted account with dangling references.

BAR-143.title: Authoritative state lives in a durable store distinct from the serving process
BAR-143.statement: Replacing the serving process entirely — rolling it to a fresh instance with no shared memory — without touching the data store leaves all accounts, chirps, follows, likes, and active sessions intact afterward, demonstrating that the authoritative state did not live in the replaced process.

BAR-144.title: The persistence seam is backed by a durable store, closing the in-memory blocker
BAR-144.statement: The persistence seam the product reads and writes through (the `ChirpRepository` boundary in `chirp-server`, or its equivalent) is backed by a durable store rather than process memory on the released product, confirmed by the product's state surviving a restart. The in-memory backing at `Nousix-LLC/nswe-demo @ c805525` is the named release blocker this closes; the store engine, schema, and migrations are deferred to the code work and are not fixed here.

BAR-145.title: Readiness reflects durable-store availability
BAR-145.statement: The product reports ready to serve only when its durable store is reachable: queried while the store is unreachable to the serving process it reports not-ready, and queried while the store is reachable and the product can serve it reports ready.
BAR-145.proposed: releasable ### Persistence — backup, recovery, and a person's own copy

BAR-146.title: Durable data can be backed up and restored intact
BAR-146.statement: A backup produced from a populated deployment can be restored, and on the restored store the accounts, chirps, follows, and likes are present and satisfy every model invariant — references resolve, ids are unchanged, counts equal the edges.

BAR-147.title: Durable data is enumerable per account for export
BAR-147.statement: For a signed-in account, the product can produce that account's profile, its complete set of chirps, and its complete set of followed accounts, matching the committed durable state at the time of the request.

BAR-148.title: Upgrading the product preserves existing durable data
BAR-148.statement: After an upgrade that changes the shape of the data (a redeploy with a data-model change), the accounts, chirps, follows, and likes that existed before the upgrade are all present afterward and their references still resolve.

BAR-160.title: The product is the four-crate, two-layer partition with every responsibility assigned once
BAR-160.statement: The product is exactly a client-side framework layer (`ferric` with `ferric-http` and `ferric-router`) and a product layer of three crates (`chirp-types`, `chirp-server`, `chirp-frontend`), with no fifth product crate silently carrying responsibility, and for every entity its wire shape, its lifecycle and persistence, and its presentation each resolve to exactly one part (no entity owned by two parts, none owned by the frontend).

BAR-161.title: `ferric` carries no chirp domain knowledge and the dependency direction is one-way
BAR-161.statement: The `ferric` crates reference no chirp entity (account, chirp, follow, like, timeline, session) and do not depend on `chirp-types`; `chirp-frontend` depends on the `ferric` crates and never the reverse.

BAR-162.title: `chirp-types` is the single source of truth for everything crossing the wire
BAR-162.statement: Every identifier, domain entity and value object, request/response shape, pagination envelope, session token, and error contract that crosses between frontend and backend is defined once in `chirp-types`; the crate carries no I/O, framework, or async dependency, so both the native backend and the WebAssembly frontend compile against the identical definitions, and no wire shape is defined anywhere else.

BAR-163.title: `chirp-server` owns the REST backend and enforces the domain invariants
BAR-163.statement: Against the running product, actions that would violate a domain invariant (following oneself, liking a chirp twice, posting as a nonexistent account) are refused with a categorized error and no violating state is stored; `chirp-server` is the authority that enforces these invariants.

BAR-164.title: Domain rules are enforced on the server, not trusted from the client
BAR-164.statement: Submitting directly to the API, bypassing the frontend, a chirp over the length limit, a self-follow, and a chirp attributed to a nonexistent account is refused by the server regardless of any client-side checking.

BAR-165.title: All durable state flows through one replaceable persistence boundary
BAR-165.statement: A single `ChirpRepository` boundary in `chirp-server` mediates every durable operation and enumerates exactly the durable operations the product uses; no handler or frontend code reaches around it to the store, and a durable store added as a second implementation requires no change to any handler.

BAR-166.title: One process serves the API, the app, and the health endpoint
BAR-166.statement: From one address, the running service serves the REST API, loads the single-page app, and answers the health endpoint; no second process or second deployable is required to serve the app.

BAR-167.title: The frontend holds only session state and no durable state
BAR-167.statement: The only state `chirp-frontend` owns across views is the current session (the authenticated account and its bearer token); every account, chirp, follow, like, and timeline it shows is fetched from the backend through the typed API client, and reloading the app re-fetches state so no entity data persists only in the client.
BAR-167.proposed: usable_early ### Modules — the REST contract (frontend↔server seam)
BAR-167.final: usable_early ### Modules — the REST contract (frontend↔server seam)

BAR-168.title: There is exactly one typed client↔server contract
BAR-168.statement: The frontend and server build requests and decode responses from the same `chirp-types` definitions, with no second, hand-maintained copy of any wire shape on either side.

BAR-169.title: The API is namespaced and same-origin with the app
BAR-169.statement: The REST surface lives under a reserved path prefix reached on the same origin that served the app, so no cross-origin configuration is part of normal operation; a path that is not an API path resolves to the single-page app rather than an API handler.

BAR-170.title: The contract covers the core-loop operations the app depends on
BAR-170.statement: Create an account, fetch an account's public profile, open a session, post a chirp (including a reply), read a timeline, follow and unfollow an account, and like and unlike a chirp are each served end to end from the app and each has a defined request and response type in the contract.

BAR-171.title: Timeline reads cross the contract as bounded pages behind an opaque cursor
BAR-171.statement: A timeline read over the API returns a bounded page with an opaque continuation cursor when more chirps remain, passing the cursor returns the next older page, and a requested size above the server's maximum is clamped so a client cannot pull every chirp in one response.

BAR-172.title: Authentication crosses as an opaque bearer token; private data never crosses outward
BAR-172.statement: A signed-in request proves itself by presenting the session as an opaque bearer token the server issued, and only an account's public profile fields and public chirps cross the contract outward — credential, verified contact, and session data never appear in any response.

BAR-173.title: Errors cross the contract as a typed, machine-readable category
BAR-173.statement: A failed request returns a typed error carrying a machine-readable category (for example validation, not-found, conflict, unauthorized, forbidden) the frontend can branch on — distinguishing, for instance, a taken handle from a malformed one — rather than an ad-hoc string.

BAR-174.title: The contract's wire conventions are stable and grow additively
BAR-174.statement: JSON field names are stable regardless of internal renames, opaque identifiers and tokens serialize as their bare value, validated value objects reject invalid input on the way in, and error categories are machine-readable constants; the contract's public surface grows only by addition, and changing or removing an existing wire shape is out of bounds.

BAR-175.title: New release surfaces extend the one contract, not a second API
BAR-175.statement: Each new surface the release adopts — among them ending a session, editing a profile, account settings, recovery, data export, account deletion, reporting and blocking/muting, notifications, an operator/administrative surface, and a way to find accounts to follow — has its request/response types defined in `chirp-types` and its operations mounted under the one namespaced API alongside the existing ones, not in a separate contract or service.
BAR-175.proposed: releasable ### Modules — delivery and entry points
BAR-175.final: releasable ### Modules — delivery and entry points

BAR-176.title: The app is served as static assets with a single-page fallback and owns its routing
BAR-176.statement: `chirp-server` serves the frontend as static assets from a configurable root, a request to an in-app route reached directly loads the app and resolves that route client-side, and a request for an unknown path returns the app's entry document rather than a server error.

BAR-177.title: The product has one user entry point: a single web address
BAR-177.statement: A person reaches the product at one web address that serves the single-page app, with nothing to install and no second place to go, and the in-app route set reaches the release's surfaces (sign-up, sign-in, recovery, settings, deletion, and the rest) rather than adding a separate app.

BAR-178.title: The health/readiness entry point reports readiness, not just liveness
BAR-178.statement: An operator can query an unauthenticated health endpoint with no session; with the durable store made unavailable it reports not-ready, and with the service able to serve users it reports ready, so an orchestrator can tell "serving" from "merely running."

BAR-179.title: The service is configured from the environment and ships as one artifact
BAR-179.statement: The service's network bind address and static-asset root are read from the environment with sensible defaults rather than hard-coded, and the product ships as one self-contained artifact serving both the API and the app that deploys to a fresh environment by setting configuration only, without editing source.

BAR-200.statement: With no session, every signed-out screen (at minimum the landing and a public profile opened by direct link) carries the chirp wordmark, a Sign in entry, a prominent Sign up entry, and footer access to the rules and to help; from each, a person can act (sign in, sign up, read the rules, reach help) without first being signed in and without reaching a dead end.

BAR-201.statement: Signed in, a persistent shell exposes Home, Explore, Notifications, Profile, Settings, and a Compose affordance, and all six are reachable from every signed-in screen — verified from the timeline, a profile, a conversation, and a settings sub-section — without using the browser back control.

BAR-202.statement: On every screen the product shows where the person is: navigating to Home, Explore, Notifications, Profile, and a settings sub-section in turn, the active primary-nav destination is visibly marked and the browser tab title (and the screen's main heading) names the current screen.

BAR-203.statement: Every screen the product presents, signed-out and signed-in, matches a published screen-inventory entry (route, exactly one archetype, declared auth state); no presented screen is absent from the inventory, and every signed-in-reachable inventory screen can in fact be reached.

BAR-204.statement: Signed in and starting from the home timeline, a person reaches each of compose, their own profile, notifications, settings, explore, help, and the rules in no more than two steps through the product, without holding an external link.

BAR-205.statement: A public profile and an individual chirp's conversation each resolve from a stable, shareable URL that, opened directly in a fresh browser context, lands on that exact profile / that exact chirp — not on a generic home or a redirect to sign-in for public content.

BAR-206.statement: Opening a signed-in-only URL (for example a settings sub-section) with no session routes the person to sign-in, and after a successful sign-in lands them on that originally requested screen rather than on a default screen such as the home timeline.

BAR-207.statement: An action taken with an expired or invalid session (for example opening the timeline or submitting a drafted chirp) routes the person to sign-in with the reason stated, does not lose their in-progress input, and returns them to where they were after they sign back in.

BAR-208.statement: The browser back control returns to the previous screen without re-submitting the prior action and without losing the person's place in a scrolled timeline, and a dialog counts as one step so that back dismisses it by closing it; pressing back after posting a chirp does not re-post it.

BAR-209.statement: A list with more items than one page loads a bounded first page rather than every item at once, offers an explicit way to load older items, and — on the timeline — offers a way to pull in chirps posted since the person opened it.

BAR-210.statement: Every irreversible or destructive action — delete account, delete a chirp, block or mute, end a session, sign out of all sessions — presents an explicit confirmation that names the consequence and offers a cancel before it proceeds, and cancelling changes nothing; the account-deletion confirmation additionally states what is and is not retained and points to data export.

BAR-211.statement: Every completed action (for example publishing a chirp, following an account, saving a setting) shows brief, non-blocking confirmation, and every failed action is shown at the point it was taken — against the field for a form, against the control for an in-place action — with enough to understand and retry; no action completes or fails silently.

BAR-212.statement: A signed-in person can start composing a chirp from any screen through a persistent compose affordance without navigating away first (verified from the timeline, a profile, and notifications), and opening the dedicated compose URL directly opens the compose surface.

BAR-213.statement: A completed sign-up establishes the session and lands the person on onboarding — not on a repeated sign-in prompt and not on a blank timeline; and signing out ends the session, returns the person to the signed-out landing, and leaves the browser back control unable to re-expose a protected screen's content.

BAR-214.statement: Account-level choices live under one settings area with labelled sub-sections (edit profile, account & contact, notification preferences, sessions & devices, blocked & muted, export, delete), each opening directly by its own URL and each returning to the settings hub; and the rules/terms and a user-facing help & support entry are reachable from both the signed-out shell and the signed-in shell.

BAR-215.title: Unrelated screens share one visual treatment
BAR-215.statement: On three screens of different archetypes on the live product (for example the home timeline, a profile, and a settings sub-section), body text is the same size and leading, the gutters and spacing rhythm match, buttons share one shape and one primary colour, and no screen introduces a colour or control style absent from the others.

BAR-216.title: Reading text is legible and hierarchy is visible
BAR-216.statement: On the live product, chirp and reading text renders at no less than 15px with visibly generous line spacing; on any screen the main heading is visibly larger and heavier than its body text, and meta text (timestamps, handles) is visibly quieter than body text.

BAR-217.title: Colour contrast meets WCAG 2.1 AA, measured
BAR-217.statement: On the live product, sample body text, secondary text, link text, primary-button text, and a field border and measure each with a contrast tool: normal text reaches ≥ 4.5:1, large text ≥ 3:1, and control and meaningful-icon boundaries ≥ 3:1. The measurement passes in each theme the product ships.

BAR-218.title: Every keyboard-reachable control shows a visible focus indicator
BAR-218.statement: Using only the keyboard on the live product, tabbing through a screen's links, buttons, fields, and menu items shows a distinct focus indicator on each that stands out from its surroundings, and no focusable control takes focus without a visible indicator.

BAR-219.title: Spacing, grid, and reading measure are consistent and bounded
BAR-219.statement: On the live product, the reading column (timeline, conversation, profile chirps, a form) is held to a bounded measure on a wide window rather than spanning the whole width; on a phone viewport the same content fills the width with a consistent edge gutter; and the spacing between items is visibly uniform within and across these screens.

BAR-220.title: Overlapping surfaces stack in a consistent order
BAR-220.statement: On the live product, opening a menu places it above content; opening a dialog places it above content on a dimmed scrim with the menu not showing through; triggering a toast places it above the dialog. At no point does a lower layer render on top of a higher one.

BAR-221.title: Icons are consistent and meaning never rides on colour alone
BAR-221.statement: On the live product, icons come from one consistent set; the current primary-nav destination reads as active by more than colour, confirmed still identifiable in greyscale or a colour-blind simulation; and every icon-only control (compose, like, menu) exposes an accessible name to a screen reader and a label on hover.

BAR-222.title: Motion is bounded and respects reduced-motion
BAR-222.statement: On the live product, opening and closing a menu and a dialog and triggering a toast each complete a brief transition (well under half a second) that settles, with nothing animating or blinking continuously apart from a bounded loading indicator; with the system reduce-motion setting on, the same actions remove or reduce animation to a short fade and no information is lost.

BAR-223.title: One voice, with plain and actionable errors
BAR-223.statement: On the live product, action buttons across several screens read as sentence-case verbs (for example "Post", "Follow", "Save changes") rather than "OK"/"Submit" or Title Case; and a forced error (an invalid form entry, then a failed submit) shows a plain-language message with a way forward and no raw error code, stack text, or internal identifier.

BAR-224.title: Screens are assembled from the named components, and components come from the tokens
BAR-224.statement: On three screens of different archetypes on the live product, a chirp, buttons, text fields, and error messages each render from one shared treatment with no bespoke control standing in for a library component; and inspecting a chirp card, a primary button, a text field, and a dialog in each shipped theme shows colours matching the token roles (a primary action is the one primary colour, a destructive one the danger colour), text sizes matching the type scale, and no colour or size that is absent from the token set.

BAR-225.title: The chirp card and compose box hold the core-loop contract
BAR-225.statement: On the live product, typing past the character limit in compose turns the counter to the danger treatment and disables Post; an empty draft leaves Post disabled and posts nothing; a valid chirp posts and appears as a chirp card showing avatar, author, handle, relative time, text, and the like / reply / more-actions row; and liking a chirp shows a filled icon and a "Liked" label together, still identifiable as liked in greyscale.

BAR-226.title: Empty, loading, and failure states carry a designed treatment
BAR-226.statement: On the live product, a brand-new account's empty timeline shows an explanatory block with a next step rather than a blank area; a list while loading shows skeleton rows at the real item size rather than a spinner on a blank screen; a forced page-load failure shows an inline message with a retry in place of the missing items while keeping any items already shown; and a failed action shows an inline error in the product's danger styling at the point of action. None of these renders a blank area, a frozen screen, or a raw failure.

BAR-227.title: Forms validate inline at the field, in plain language
BAR-227.statement: On the live product sign-up, submitting a handle already in use shows a plain-language error against the handle field naming the handle (not in a distant summary and not as a code); submitting a mis-formatted handle shows a field-level validation error that explains the rule; and while a handle's availability is being checked the field shows a pending state rather than flicking prematurely to valid or invalid.

BAR-228.title: Consequential actions are confirmed before they happen
BAR-228.statement: On the live product, initiating deletion of a chirp, blocking an account, and deleting the account each present a confirmation that names what will happen and offers a plain cancel, and nothing changes on cancel; the account-deletion confirmation additionally states what is and is not retained and points to data export before proceeding.

BAR-229.title: The result of every action is shown through the feedback components
BAR-229.statement: On the live product, publishing a chirp, following an account, and saving a setting each show a brief, non-blocking confirmation; an action in flight shows its control in a busy state that cannot be re-triggered; and a forced in-place failure (acting while offline, or a transient server error while posting) shows the failure at the control with a way to retry and does not lose the drafted text.

BAR-230.statement: With no session, opening the site root reaches a Landing that says what chirp is and shows both a Sign up and a Sign in action, each reachable without first signing in. Where a public sample is served it shows real public chirps; where none is served the Landing still explains chirp and offers both actions rather than a blank area.

BAR-231.statement: The Sign up screen collects a handle, a display name, an optional bio marked optional, a credential, and a point of contact — and no fields beyond these — and on submit with valid values creates the account and signs the person in. The contact is shown as pending verification and is not treated as confirmed until it is verified.

BAR-232.statement: On the Sign up screen a handle that is already taken, or that breaks the rule (more than 15 characters, or anything other than letters, numbers, or underscores), is reported inline against the handle field so the person can fix it before submitting, and a valid unused handle resolves to accepted. The check does not disclose which other handles exist beyond the conflict it reports.

BAR-233.statement: Signing in requires the credential set at sign-up or recovery — a known handle alone never grants a session. A handle that matches no account returns a not-found result with a path to Sign up; a real handle with a wrong credential returns a failed sign-in the person can retry or recover from, with a path to Recover access. Neither result reveals account existence beyond what a public profile already shows, and neither shows a system code.

BAR-234.statement: A person who cannot sign in can start recovery themselves from a Recover access screen that runs through the account's verified contact. Submitting a contact returns the same neutral acknowledgement whether or not it matches an account, so the response discloses no account existence. Following a valid recovery step opens a Set new credential screen, and after setting a new credential the person is routed to Sign in and can sign in with it. An expired or already-used recovery link is explained with a path back to Recover access rather than a dead end.

BAR-235.statement: Signing out is confirmed before it proceeds; the confirmation names the consequence and offers both a cancel and an option to end sessions on all other devices. Confirming ends the current session on the server — the prior session can no longer be used — and lands the person on the signed-out Landing. Cancelling changes nothing. A sign-out that fails is reported and leaves the person signed in rather than appearing to succeed.

BAR-236.statement: Each of the Landing, Sign up, Sign in, Recover access, Set new credential, and Sign out surfaces presents a designed state for empty, loading, and error — a field-level message, a busy control, a skeleton, or an explained error with a next step — rather than a blank area, a hang, or a silent failure. Where a state does not apply to a surface, that is stated rather than left undesigned.

BAR-237.statement: A completed sign-up lands the person on the onboarding screen, not a sign-in prompt or a blank page. A person routed from a signed-in-only screen to Sign in lands back on the screen they asked for after signing in. After signing out, pressing back does not show the protected screen's content. (The three-way links among Sign in, Sign up, and Recover access ride the non-gating REQ-UX-015 and are not part of this release condition; a first release may omit them provided Recover access stays reachable from Help & support.)

BAR-238.statement: A signed-in person who opens the home destination sees a timeline carrying their own chirps and the chirps of the accounts they follow, ordered newest first, and the signed-in shell marks Home as the current destination. The timeline arrives as a bounded first page with a visible control to load older chirps; using that control brings in a further bounded page, and at no point does the product load the entire timeline in one request. Following at least one account that has posted, the person sees those chirps interleaved with their own in newest-first order.

BAR-239.statement: When chirps have been posted since the person last viewed the timeline, a catch-up control at the top of the list states how many new chirps are waiting and, when used, brings them in as a single bounded step that returns the reader to the newest chirps — not an open-ended scroll back through everything missed. Opening a chirp's conversation and returning to the timeline leaves the reader at the position they left, not reset to the top of the list.

BAR-240.statement: The home timeline shows a designed state for empty, for failure, and for loading in place of a blank region or an indefinite spinner. An account that follows no one and has posted nothing sees an empty state that explains why the timeline is empty and offers a route to Explore and to composing a first chirp. A failed first page shows a plain-language message with a retry in place of the list, visibly distinct from the empty state; a failed load-older or failed catch-up is shown at the boundary while the chirps already on screen stay loaded. A first load shows skeleton rows at the size of real chirp cards while the signed-in shell stays visible, and no region of the timeline continues to spin without resolving.

BAR-241.statement: The compose surface shows a remaining-character count that warns as the 280-character limit nears and marks the draft as over the limit once it is exceeded. The post action is not activatable while the draft is empty or over the limit, and an empty or over-limit submission reached by any path creates no chirp. While a publish is in flight the post action shows a busy state and the same draft cannot be submitted a second time; on success the chirp is published, the field clears, and a brief non-blocking confirmation is shown; on failure the draft text is kept exactly as written with an inline error and a retry, so the person can post again without retyping. No successful post is duplicated and no failed post loses its draft.

BAR-242.statement: The compose surface is reachable inline at the top of the home timeline, as the Compose dialog (opened from the signed-in shell's compose affordance and directly at `/compose`), and in the reply position of a chirp's conversation screen, and it behaves the same way in each. In every placement an untouched field shows a placeholder prompt, a remaining-character count at the full 280 budget, and a disabled primary action; the action is labelled for its placement — "Post" when writing a chirp, "Reply" when answering one. Dismissing the Compose dialog with text still in the field and reopening it does not lose the draft.

BAR-243.statement: Signed in on a chirp's conversation, a person can write a reply within the character limit and publish it from the conversation's reply control; the published reply then appears in that conversation shown as answering the chirp, and its publication is confirmed. Attempting to reply to a chirp that no longer exists reports not-found at the reply control and keeps the typed draft, rather than appearing to send. Opened without a session, the conversation presents a visible way to sign in or sign up in place of the reply control, not a dead or silent one.

BAR-244.statement: A chirp's like control toggles between not-liked and liked, with the liked state distinguished by more than colour (a filled heart and a "Liked" label). Liking an already-liked chirp, or reloading the screen, does not raise the count a second time; unliking returns the count to its earlier value. When a like or unlike cannot be completed, the control returns to its prior state, the count is left unchanged (it never shows a like that did not take), and the failure is reported at the control with a way to retry. The control looks and behaves the same wherever the chirp is shown — in the timeline, in its conversation, and on a profile.

BAR-245.statement: On another person's profile header or in a person row, the follow control toggles between "Follow" and "Following"; following the same account again, or reloading, leaves exactly one follow in place with the control reading "Following", and unfollowing returns it to "Follow". A person's own identity never presents a Follow control — the own-identity action is "Edit profile" — so a self-follow cannot be started, and any attempt is refused and shown at the control. When a follow or unfollow cannot be completed, the control returns to its prior label, any follower count is unchanged, and the failure is reported at the control with a way to retry. The control looks and behaves the same wherever it appears (profile header and person rows).

BAR-246.statement: A person's profile at its handle URL shows their avatar, display name, handle, bio, and follower and following counts, above that person's own chirps in newest-first bounded pages with a way to load older ones, and loads both without a session and with one; signed in, the header also carries the follow control. When the signed-in owner opens their own profile, they see the same public face a visitor sees, with an "Edit profile" entry in place of the follow control that opens the edit-profile screen, and no follow control is shown on their own profile.

BAR-247.statement: A profile's follower and following counts open the followers list and the following list, each at its own URL. Each list shows one person per row with enough to recognise the account (avatar, display name, handle, bio) in a bounded page with a way to load more, a labelled way back to the profile, and — for a signed-in viewer — a follow control on each row. Each list's URL, opened directly, lands on that list.

BAR-248.statement: After a fresh sign-up, a brand-new account lands on the onboarding screen and sees, in plain language, why its timeline is empty and at least one working control that opens compose to write a first chirp (and, wherever discovery is present, a control to find people to follow). The explanation and the compose route appear immediately and stay usable while any suggestions preview is still loading — shown as placeholders, not a blank region — and after that preview fails or comes back empty. The screen is never a blank page and never leaves the person without a next step.

BAR-249.statement: A signed-in person can reach edit profile from the settings hub and from the edit action on their own profile, change their display name and bio, and save; the saved values then show on their profile. An empty required display name or a rejected value is reported against the field in plain words and no save is made; a save that fails is reported at the form with the person's edited values still present so they can retry; a save that succeeds is confirmed. The screen never reports success or failure silently and never shows a raw system or error code.

BAR-250.statement: A signed-in person opening settings sees a labelled row for every account section in the release — edit profile, account & contact, sessions & devices, blocked & muted, export your data, and delete account (the notification-preferences row appears only where notifications are in the release). Each row opens its section both by selection and by entering the section's own URL directly in a fresh tab, and each section offers a labelled way back to the hub that works alongside the browser back control. The delete-account row is shown as destructive and opens a confirmation rather than deleting when selected. If the account summary fails to load, every section row is still reachable.

BAR-251.statement: On the account & contact screen a signed-in person sees their current point of contact with a status of either "Verified" or "Not verified yet". They can change the contact and save; the change is confirmed, the new contact shows as not-yet-verified, and the screen offers a step that confirms the person controls it before it is used for account recovery. An unverified contact is presented as a caution, not an error, and is not treated as verified until that step is completed. A failed save is shown against the contact field with the typed value preserved for retry.

BAR-252.statement: A signed-in person opening sessions & devices sees every place the account is currently signed in, each with enough to recognise it — device and browser, approximate location, last-active time — and the current session marked. Ending another session goes through a confirmation that names the effect; after confirming, that session leaves the list and the next action attempted from the ended session on its own device is refused and requires a fresh sign-in.

BAR-253.statement: A signed-in person can sign out from sessions & devices through a confirmation that, where the account is signed in elsewhere, offers to end those other sessions too. After sign-out the person is on the signed-out landing; the browser back control does not re-expose any protected screen; and replaying the signed-out session's request is refused, so the next person at that device is not signed in as them.

BAR-254.statement: From the export screen a signed-in person sees what the export contains and a single request action. After requesting, the screen shows a preparing state rather than freezing or blanking, and when ready offers a way to download the file; the downloaded file opens outside chirp and contains the person's chirps, their profile, and who they follow. A preparation that fails is explained in plain words with a retry, and no broken file is offered.

BAR-255.statement: The delete-account confirmation, shown before anything is deleted, states plainly that the account and its chirps are removed and cannot be recovered, shows what is and is not retained and what happens to the handle (matching the product's stated deletion outcome), and points the person to export their data first. The delete action stays unavailable until the person gives the explicit confirmation it asks for. Cancelling at any point returns to settings with the account and its content unchanged and still able to sign in. Giving the confirmation and deleting signs the person out to the signed-out landing, after which the account can no longer sign in and the browser back control does not re-expose the deleted account's screens.

BAR-256.statement: Signed in, a person can open the report action from both a chirp's and an account's more-actions menu, choose a reason, add optional detail, and submit, and sees an in-product confirmation that the report was received; and when no reason is chosen the submit control does not send the report. No report path ends in a silent no-op.

BAR-257.statement: From both the signed-out and the signed-in shell, a person can reach a Rules & terms screen that lists the product's rules as named categories; and the reasons offered in the report action correspond to those same named categories, so a submitted report points at a stated rule rather than an unlabelled choice.

BAR-258.statement: A Help & support entry is reachable with no session from the signed-out shell and, signed in, from the account menu; from it a person can reach the recover-access path ("Can't get in?") and a way to contact the operator ("Contact support") for what self-service does not cover.

BAR-259.statement: Opening an address that does not resolve — a mistyped path, a deleted chirp, an unavailable account — shows a not-found screen that states the resource is missing (consistent with the in-place tombstone used elsewhere), reveals no private detail about a removed or restricted resource, and offers a route to a known place (the home timeline when signed in, the landing when signed out) rather than a broken page.

BAR-260.statement: On each surface in this area a person can force an empty result, a failed load, and a first load and sees, respectively, an explained empty treatment carrying at least one next step (never a blank region), a distinct "couldn't load — try again" treatment with a retry, and a loading treatment — with the empty treatment and the failed treatment visibly different from each other; a surface to which one of these states does not apply says so rather than showing nothing. Checked across, for example, Notifications, the report and block/mute dialogs on a failed submit (the dialog stays open with its input preserved and an inline error), the blocked & muted screen when empty, a brand-new home timeline, and an empty followers list.

BAR-261.statement: On a slow connection a first load of a content surface shows skeletons sized to the real content — not a spinner on a blank page — while the persistent navigation frame stays visible; an incremental load, such as loading older items, shows a bounded indicator at the point of the action while the already-loaded content stays on screen; and a load that cannot resolve stops and becomes an error with a retry rather than spinning without end.

BAR-262.statement: A person who triggers a field error (for example a taken handle at sign-up), a failed in-place action (for example a like or follow that fails), and a failed list page sees in each case a plain-language message at the point of the problem — no system or error code, never a silent no-op and never a blank — with a way to retry or correct and their input preserved; an optimistic in-place action that fails reverts to its prior state rather than showing a result that did not happen.

BAR-263.statement: With a session expired, a person who drafts a chirp and tries to post is routed to sign-in with the reason stated — not a silent failure — and, after signing in, is returned to where they were with the drafted text intact; and a transient server error during the same post can be retried in place and succeeds without re-typing the draft. This observes, and does not redefine, the information architecture's session-expiry (REQ-UX-008) and auth-gated-return (REQ-UX-007) conventions.

CSS px throughout.

BAR-265.title: The whole core loop completes on a phone
BAR-265.statement: At a 360×640 CSS-px portrait viewport, signed in, a person completes the whole core loop end to end — open and scroll the home timeline, open Compose and post a chirp, reply to a chirp, like then unlike a chirp, follow then unfollow an account, and open a public profile — and at no step is there horizontal page scrolling, a control hidden off-screen, or an action target that cannot be tapped.

BAR-266.title: One reading column that reflows, not rescales, across viewports
BAR-266.statement: The content region is a single reading column at every width. At a 360px-wide viewport it fills the width inside the 16px gutter with no horizontal scrollbar; at a 1280px-wide viewport it is held to the 600px measure and horizontally centred, not stretched across the window. Neither width requires pinch-zoom or sideways scrolling to read a chirp.

BAR-267.title: The signed-in navigation shell adapts and keeps every destination reachable
BAR-267.statement: Signed in, starting from the timeline, a person reaches Home, Explore, Notifications, Profile, Settings, and a Compose affordance, and sees the current destination marked, at both a compact (< 640px) and a wide (≥ 1024px) viewport: at compact width the primary destinations sit in a bottom tab bar and Compose is reachable without opening a menu; at wide width the same destinations appear in a persistent side navigation.

BAR-268.title: The signed-out shell never dead-ends at any viewport
BAR-268.statement: With no session, the Landing and a public profile link each show a Sign up and a Sign in entry without opening a menu, and keep Rules & terms and Help & support reachable (at minimum by scrolling to the footer), at both a compact (< 640px) and a wide (≥ 1024px) viewport. No viewport presents an authentication wall or hides the path to join.

BAR-269.title: Feed and list screens adapt without losing their controls or scroll place
BAR-269.statement: On a compact (< 640px) viewport, a feed/list screen longer than one page (home timeline, a chirp's conversation, notifications, search results, followers, following) keeps its load-older control and its "N new chirps" catch-up reachable without horizontal scrolling and keeps each chirp card's reply, like, and more controls tappable; opening an item and pressing back restores the list at its prior scroll position.

BAR-270.title: Form screens are usable with the on-screen keyboard
BAR-270.statement: On a compact (< 640px) viewport with the on-screen keyboard open, a form screen (sign up, sign in, recover access, set new credential, edit profile) shows the focused field, its label, and any inline error together; keeps its primary submit reachable by scrolling the form without first dismissing the keyboard; and never requires horizontal scrolling or a side-by-side field layout. An invalid field's error shows with the field, not in a summary elsewhere.

BAR-271.title: Profile and settings screens stack and keep a labelled way back
BAR-271.statement: On a compact (< 640px) viewport a public profile shows the header's avatar, display name, handle, bio, counts, and its context action (Follow, or Edit profile on one's own profile) without horizontal scrolling, with the chirps list in one column below; the Settings hub and each sub-section are full screens, and a labelled back returns from a sub-section to the hub.

BAR-272.title: Overlays present as full-height surfaces on a phone with their actions reachable
BAR-272.statement: On a compact (< 640px) viewport, Compose and Report present as a full-screen or bottom-sheet surface whose input and primary action stay visible and operable with the keyboard open, and every destructive confirmation (delete account, delete chirp, block or mute, end a session, sign out) shows both its confirm and its cancel fully visible and tappable without clipping at the screen edge; the browser back control dismisses the overlay without leaving the underlying screen.

BAR-273.title: Touch targets are large enough and within thumb reach
BAR-273.statement: On a touch viewport every interactive control renders a tap target of at least 44×44 CSS px with at least 8 CSS px between adjacent targets, and the core-loop primary actions (the Compose affordance, a chirp card's like and reply controls, and the primary navigation) render within the lower portion of the screen rather than only at the top.

BAR-274.title: No auto-zoom and no horizontal scroll, portrait and landscape
BAR-274.statement: Walking the signed-in core loop at a supported phone viewport in portrait and then in landscape, the page never scrolls horizontally and never needs pinch-zoom, and focusing a sign-in or compose text field does not trigger the browser's automatic zoom; content reflows to the narrower dimension rather than overflowing it.

Each criterion names the specific thing a reviewer checks on the live product and how, never "accessible" in the abstract.
BAR-274.final: usable_early --- ## Accessibility — `BAR-275..294` The committed standard is WCAG 2.1 Level AA over the gated conformance set (the core loop and the get-in screens with their empty, loading, and error states). Each criterion names the specific thing a reviewer checks on the live product and how, never "accessible" in the abstract.

BAR-275.title: The committed standard and the gated set are stated by name
BAR-275.statement: The product states its accessibility standard as WCAG 2.1 Level AA by name (not "accessible" in the abstract) and names its gated conformance set — the core loop and the get-in screens (sign-up, sign-in, recovery, onboarding) with their empty, loading, and error states. A reviewer can find the stated standard and the enumerated gated set in the product's accessibility statement.

BAR-276.title: The core loop and get-in flows are operable by keyboard alone
BAR-276.statement: With the pointer unused, a keyboard-only user completes every core-loop and get-in action: sign in, read the timeline, operate a chirp's reply/like/more controls, compose and post a chirp, follow an account, open a profile, and operate a settings sub-section. No action is reachable by pointer only.

BAR-277.title: Focus order is logical and focus is always visible
BAR-277.statement: Tabbing through the timeline, a form, and a settings screen, focus moves in each screen's reading order and the focused control always shows a visible focus indicator. Opening a dialog moves focus into it; closing it returns focus to the opening control; changing route lands focus on the new screen rather than on a removed control.

BAR-278.title: No keyboard trap; modal focus is held but escapable
BAR-278.statement: No screen leaves keyboard focus stuck with no way out. A modal dialog (compose, a destructive confirmation) holds focus while open, cycles focus within itself on Tab, closes on Esc and on its close/Cancel control, and returns focus to the control that opened it.

BAR-279.title: A skip control bypasses the navigation shell to the content
BAR-279.statement: On a signed-in screen, one Tab from the top reveals a visible "Skip to content" control that moves focus past the navigation shell to the main content, and a screen reader can jump to the main landmark directly.

BAR-280.title: Every control exposes a name, a role, and its state
BAR-280.statement: With a screen reader, each interactive component — chirp card, compose box, text field, toggle, button, icon button, dialog — is announced with a sensible accessible name, its correct role (button, switch, text box, dialog), and its current state (a like as pressed or not, a toggle as on or off, a busy or disabled control as such).

BAR-281.title: Each screen exposes landmark regions
BAR-281.statement: With a screen reader, the landing, the timeline, and a settings sub-section each expose a navigation landmark, exactly one main landmark, and (on the signed-out shell) a footer landmark, and the user can jump between them.

BAR-282.title: One top-level heading per screen, nested in order
BAR-282.statement: With a screen reader, the heading list for the timeline, a profile, and a settings sub-section each shows exactly one top-level heading that names the screen and matches the browser tab title, with sub-headings descending in order and no skipped levels.

BAR-283.title: Lists and feeds are navigable as lists
BAR-283.statement: With a screen reader on the timeline, the feed is navigable item by item — each chirp is a distinguishable list item the reader can tell from the next — and the "load older" and "N new chirps" catch-up affordances are reported as named buttons. The conversation, notifications, search-results, and followers/following lists expose the same item structure.

BAR-284.title: Icon-only controls expose a text label and their active state
BAR-284.statement: With a screen reader, each icon-only control (the compose affordance, a like control, the current nav destination) reports a text name; the like reports pressed or not-pressed and the current nav destination reports its selected state as a programmatic state, not by colour or fill alone.

BAR-285.title: Contrast meets AA in every shipped theme
BAR-285.statement: An automated contrast scan run against the live product in each shipped theme finds normal text at or above 4.5:1, large text at or above 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.3), and meaningful control and icon boundaries at or above 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11), with no reported failure.

BAR-286.title: Text resizes and the page reflows without loss
BAR-286.statement: At 200% browser zoom the timeline and a form show no clipped content and keep every control reachable (WCAG 1.4.4); at a 320-CSS-pixel viewport the reading content reflows to one column with no horizontal scrolling (WCAG 1.4.10); and an applied text-spacing override clips or overlaps nothing (WCAG 1.4.12).

BAR-287.title: No fact is carried by colour alone
BAR-287.statement: Viewed in greyscale or a colour-blindness simulation, a field error, an active like, and the current nav destination are each still identifiable without their colour — carried by text, an icon, or a label as well (WCAG 1.4.1).

BAR-288.title: No content flashes more than three times a second
BAR-288.statement: Through normal use of the product, no content flashes more than three times in any one second (WCAG 2.3.1).

BAR-289.title: Reduced motion is honoured with no loss of information
BAR-289.statement: With the system reduce-motion setting on, opening and closing a menu and a dialog, triggering a toast, and loading a list remove or shorten motion to at most a brief fade; nothing animates continuously except a loading indicator that is also announced; and no information is conveyed only by movement.

BAR-290.title: Status changes are announced without stealing focus
BAR-290.statement: With a screen reader, posting a chirp, following an account, and saving a setting are each announced as a status message through a polite live region without moving focus off the user's current control; with the timeline open, the arrival of new chirps behind the catch-up control is announced politely (WCAG 4.1.3).

BAR-291.title: Errors are announced and tied to their field
BAR-291.statement: With a screen reader on sign-up, submitting a taken handle announces the error, re-reads it when the handle field is focused, reports the field invalid, and names the problem and a fix in plain words with no error code (WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 3.3.3); a forced submit failure is announced, not silent.

BAR-292.title: Empty, loading, and expired-session states reach assistive technology
BAR-292.statement: With a screen reader, opening a list announces "loading" while its skeletons are hidden from the reader; a forced load failure announces an error with a reachable retry; a brand-new empty timeline presents a heading and a next-step action rather than silence; and acting with an expired session announces the reason and moves focus to the sign-in screen.

BAR-293.title: Conformance over the gated set is verified three ways, on a stated matrix
BAR-293.statement: For a release, three recorded checks over the gated conformance set are on file — an automated scan in each shipped theme, a keyboard-only walk, and a screen-reader walk of the core loop — together with the support matrix they ran on (at least one screen reader per major platform with its common browser), and every gated screen appears in each check.

BAR-294.title: Accessibility gates the release; failures are fixes, not waivers
BAR-294.statement: The release record shows the gated conformance set has no open Level A or Level AA failure, every accessibility failure found on the gated set was fixed rather than waived, and any failure recorded against a non-gating surface is tracked with that surface rather than blocking the release.
