BAR-300.title: A secret only the owner holds is required to sign in
BAR-300.statement: Signing in to any account requires presenting the secret established at sign-up; knowing only a handle (public information) grants no session and no authenticated action on any product surface. There is no debug route, handle-only fallback, or default/shared secret that issues a session without verifying the presented secret against the account.

BAR-301.title: A secret cannot be set weak, and guessing is slowed and silent
BAR-301.statement: A trivially weak secret (a short or well-known value) is rejected with guidance and a secret meeting the stated policy is accepted; repeated failed sign-in attempts against one account or from one source are throttled, delayed, or capped rather than answered at full speed indefinitely, and the throttled response does not distinguish "almost right" from "wrong."

BAR-302.title: No surface ever returns an account's secret
BAR-302.statement: No product surface — API response, data export, settings screen, or operator tool — returns any account's secret or holds it in a form from which the original value can be read back; the only supported way back in after losing a secret is to set a new one through recovery.

BAR-303.title: Handle format and uniqueness are enforced with field-level feedback
BAR-303.statement: Sign-up accepts a handle only if it is well-formed (up to 15 letters, digits, or underscores) and not already taken; a taken or ill-formed handle is reported as a field-level error on the handle so the person can correct it, and a valid unused handle is accepted.

BAR-304.title: Sign-in signals "no such account" vs "wrong secret" without leaking private attributes
BAR-304.statement: A sign-in with an unknown handle lets the person conclude the account does not exist (so they can proceed to sign-up); a sign-in with a known handle and a wrong secret is a retryable, recoverable failure; and neither path exposes a private attribute of any account (such as a recovery contact) beyond what the product already makes public.
BAR-304.proposed: usable_early --- ## Sessions safe to expose on the public internet
BAR-304.final: usable_early --- ## Sessions safe to expose on the public internet

BAR-305.title: The session is distinct from the secret, server-authoritative, and unforgeable
BAR-305.statement: A successful sign-in issues a session credential separate from the account secret, so routine authenticated requests never carry the secret; whether a session is valid and until when is decided server-side, and tampering with the presented session credential — altering its contents, substituting another account's identifier, or extending an encoded expiry — yields no valid or longer-lived session for any account.

BAR-306.title: Sessions expire and invalid sessions are rejected consistently
BAR-306.statement: Every session has a bounded, defined maximum lifetime after which it is rejected and the person is returned to sign-in; an expired, signed-out, or unrecognized session credential is each rejected the same way (treated as unauthenticated, with no partial or half-authenticated state); and a session accepted before a server restart behaves consistently with the expiry and invalidation rules after one.

BAR-307.title: Sign-out ends the session on the server
BAR-307.statement: A person can sign out, and sign-out invalidates the session server-side so the prior session credential can no longer act as the account — verified by replaying the prior request, which is rejected — and the next person at that device is not signed in as the previous one.

BAR-308.title: Sessions are individually identifiable and independently revocable
BAR-308.statement: A person's sessions are distinguishable from one another, so that ending one device's session rejects it on its next use while the others keep working, and the set of a person's active sessions can be listed for the account-settings surface to present.

BAR-309.title: A fresh session identity is established at sign-in (fixation resistance)
BAR-309.statement: Signing in establishes a new session identity; a session identifier carried before authentication does not become an authenticated session and carries no authenticated privileges after sign-in.

BAR-310.title: The session credential is confidential in transit and never exposed where it can be stolen
BAR-310.statement: The session credential is exchanged only over an encrypted transport — a request carrying it over an unencrypted channel is refused or redirected, never served — and it never appears in URLs, server or client logs, or storage readable by page scripts, so a network observer or an injected script cannot capture and replay it as the owner.

BAR-311.title: Every private field is encrypted in transit, product-wide
BAR-311.statement: Every private field the product exchanges with a person — the account secret at sign-up, sign-in, and recovery; the session credential; the verified contact; and the data-export payload — crosses the network only over an encrypted transport, and any request that would carry such a field in the clear is refused or redirected rather than served.
BAR-311.proposed: usable_early --- ## Authorization — who may see and change what
BAR-311.final: usable_early --- ## Authorization — who may see and change what

BAR-312.title: A valid session is the sole basis of action authority (default-deny)
BAR-312.statement: Every action that creates, changes, or removes data, and every read restricted to an owner, requires a valid authenticated session and is refused without one; any action not explicitly permitted by the authority model is refused rather than allowed by default.

BAR-313.title: The read boundary holds: public, owner-only, owner-scoped
BAR-313.statement: An account's public fields (handle, display name, bio, follower/following counts, public chirps with their reply and like counts) are readable by any viewer; its owner-only fields (verified contact, credential, active session/device list, notification preferences, settings, and any export payload) and its owner-scoped views (home timeline, account-management views) are returned only to the authenticated owner and never to another account or an unauthenticated viewer.

BAR-314.title: A person acts only as themselves, and attribution cannot be forged
BAR-314.statement: Posting, replying, liking and unliking, and following and unfollowing are authorized for and performed as the signed-in actor and cannot be directed to take effect under another account's identity; the author recorded on any chirp, reply, like, or follow is set by the product from the authenticated session, not from actor-supplied input, and no surface lets an actor create or alter content attributed to another account.

BAR-315.title: Change and removal authority is limited to the actor's own account and content
BAR-315.statement: A signed-in person can change only their own profile, contact, notification preferences, and account settings, and can delete only their own chirps and their own account; every attempt to change or delete another account or its content through any surface is refused and leaves the other account unchanged.

BAR-316.title: A refused action discloses no owner-only data or private existence
BAR-316.statement: When the authority model refuses a read or action, the response carries no owner-only field of the target account and reveals nothing about it beyond its already-public profile, and the refusal is consistent whether or not the target account exists, beyond what public lookup already discloses.
BAR-316.proposed: usable_early --- ## Managing the account: profile, settings, contact
BAR-316.final: usable_early --- ## Managing the account: profile, settings, contact

BAR-317.title: A person can edit their display name and bio
BAR-317.statement: A signed-in person can change their display name and bio under the same format rules as at sign-up; a valid change persists and shows on their public profile, and an invalid value is reported as a field-level error and not saved.

BAR-318.title: One account-settings surface gathers the account-level choices
BAR-318.statement: A signed-in person has one settings surface, reachable from the product's navigation, that presents in one place the verified contact, the active sessions/devices, and — where notifications exist — notification preferences.

BAR-319.title: The verified contact can be viewed and changed, with the change confirmed before it takes over
BAR-319.statement: From settings a person can view their current verified contact and enter a new one; the new contact becomes the recovery/notification basis only after its confirmation step is completed, and until then the prior confirmed contact remains in force.

BAR-320.title: Active sessions can be viewed and ended from settings
BAR-320.statement: From settings a person can see the sessions/devices currently signed in to their account and end any of them; an ended session can no longer act as the account.
BAR-320.proposed: releasable --- ## Getting back in: verified contact and recovery
BAR-320.final: releasable --- ## Getting back in: verified contact and recovery

BAR-321.title: A point of contact is captured at sign-up and confirmed before it is relied on
BAR-321.statement: Sign-up captures one point of contact, stores it as a private field never shown to other users, and the product confirms the person controls it before using it for recovery or notifications; an unconfirmed contact is not accepted as a basis for regaining access.

BAR-322.title: Recovery is self-service and gated on proven control of the verified contact
BAR-322.statement: A person who lost their credential can regain access themselves by proving control of the verified contact, is then prompted to set a new credential, and afterward signs in with it; the credential-reset step cannot be reached without proving contact control, and someone who does not control the contact cannot complete recovery.

BAR-323.title: Recovery does not enumerate accounts
BAR-323.statement: The recovery surface does not reveal whether a given handle or contact has an account beyond what the product already makes public; submitting a handle or contact with no account does not disclose account existence in a way that enumerates accounts.

BAR-324.title: Recovery and credential reset end the sessions that predate them
BAR-324.statement: Completing recovery and setting a new credential ends the account's sessions that predate the reset (or offers the owner the option to end them), and the old secret no longer signs in, so a recovery prompted by a possible compromise can eject an attacker.

BAR-325.title: A person can export their own data, self-service and portable, scoped to their account
BAR-325.statement: A signed-in person can obtain their own data — their chirps, profile, and follow list — through the product without contacting an operator, in a form they can open outside chirp without special tooling; the export contains only the requesting account's data and no other account's records.

BAR-326.title: An export excludes secrets and other people's private data
BAR-326.statement: A data export never includes the account's credential or session data, and never includes another person's private contact.

BAR-327.title: Account deletion is self-service, confirmed, and reversible up to confirmation
BAR-327.statement: A signed-in person can delete their own account after a confirmation that explains what will and will not survive and points to export as their chance to keep a copy; cancelling at the confirmation leaves the account and all content intact, and after deletion the account can no longer sign in.

BAR-328.title: Deletion applies the stated outcome for content and handle
BAR-328.statement: Deletion applies the product's stated outcome: the person's chirps leave public view; a reply that pointed at a now-deleted chirp shows a "chirp unavailable" placeholder with like/reply counts adjusted rather than breaking the conversation; and the freed handle is retired — not immediately re-registerable — so a departed account cannot be impersonated by someone claiming its handle.

BAR-329.title: Deletion erases private data and ends every session
BAR-329.statement: Deleting an account erases its private data — verified contact, credential, and session records — so none remains on any product surface or in an export, and immediately ends all of the account's active sessions so none can continue to act as the deleted account.

BAR-330.title: The data-rights baseline is stated and satisfied through the account's own surfaces
BAR-330.statement: The product states, where a person can find it, a data-rights baseline — access and a portable copy of their own data, and erasure by deleting their account — and every part of it is satisfied through the account's own surfaces, with no step requiring the person to contact an operator by hand.
BAR-330.proposed: releasable --- ## Operator authority (the supported admin surface)
BAR-330.final: releasable --- ## Operator authority (the supported admin surface)

BAR-331.title: Operator authority is a separate, provisioned, least-privilege role
BAR-331.statement: The authority to perform the supported administrative actions — assist recovery, remove content, action an abusive account — is provisioned outside the ordinary sign-up/sign-in path and is carried by no ordinary session; an ordinary account attempting any operator action is refused, and the operator surface exposes no authority beyond the supported set.

BAR-332.title: Operators cannot impersonate users or read credentials
BAR-332.statement: No operator action posts, replies, likes, or follows as a user, and no operator action returns any account's credential; assisting a recovery routes the user through their own verified contact rather than exposing or resetting the credential to the operator.

BAR-333.title: Operator actions are attributable, auditable, and have a defined recorded outcome
BAR-333.statement: Each operator action on an account or on content records which operator performed it, what was done, the target, and when, in a retained record not editable through the ordinary product surfaces; and operator content removal and account actioning apply the product's defined outcome (consistent with the account-deletion outcome), with the applied outcome recorded.
BAR-333.proposed: releasable --- ## Abuse resistance and the privacy floor
BAR-333.final: releasable --- ## Abuse resistance and the privacy floor

BAR-334.title: A person can report a chirp or account against stated, in-product rules
BAR-334.statement: A signed-in person can report a chirp or an account, receives an acknowledgement that the report was received, and can point the report at a specific rule; the rules that say what is and is not allowed are reachable from within the product without an external link.

BAR-335.title: Reports are captured and routed to the operator surface with enough context to act
BAR-335.statement: A filed report is recorded and made available to the authorized operator/support surface with what was reported, by whom, against whom, and which rule — enough to act on — rather than merely acknowledged to the reporter and discarded.

BAR-336.title: Rate and volume limits are a first line against flooding
BAR-336.statement: The product throttles or rejects writes and requests from one account or client that exceed a reasonable rate rather than serving them without limit, while a legitimate user at a normal rate is not blocked.

BAR-337.title: Automated account creation and mass abuse are resisted
BAR-337.statement: The product slows, challenges, or rejects automated mass account creation at the public sign-up surface and resists automated high-volume writes from many fresh accounts, while a legitimate person signing up once is not blocked.

BAR-338.title: Private fields never reach another user or a public, report, or block/mute flow
BAR-338.statement: Through every surface available to another user, to an unauthenticated visitor, and through the report/block/mute flows, only an account's public fields appear; its verified contact, credential, and session data are never returned to anyone else, and the credential is never returned to anyone in readable form.

BAR-339.title: The product collects only the data an account needs
BAR-339.statement: Every field that sign-up and the account surfaces collect and store maps to a stated account function — identity, authentication, recovery/contact, or profile — and no field is collected that no function needs.

BAR-400.statement: The deployment runs the product's authoritative state in a durable store that is a separate, persistent component from the serving process, with its own lifecycle; stopping or replacing the serving process does not stop or reset the store, and no deployment configuration keeps authoritative state only in serving-process memory. The in-memory backing of the `ChirpRepository` seam at `Nousix-LLC/nswe-demo @ c805525` does not meet this; closing it is the blocker this bar turns on.

BAR-401.statement: On a populated deployment, each of a serving-process restart, a redeploy, and a replacement of the serving process with a fresh instance leaves every Account and its Chirps, Follows, and Likes present and unchanged, with no manual step to recover them — demonstrating the authoritative state did not live in the process that was replaced.

BAR-402.statement: A create or change the product has confirmed to a person — a posted Chirp, a Follow or unfollow, a Like or unlike, a profile edit, an account deletion — is present after a restart or process replacement that happens immediately after the success response, with no further action taken. No acknowledged write is lost in the window right after its acknowledgement.

BAR-403.statement: After the serving process is restarted or replaced, the durable data still satisfies the domain invariants: every reference resolves, ids are unchanged and never reused, each Account's follower/following counts and each Chirp's like count equal their current edges, and any applied account deletion stays applied. Adding and removing a Follow and a Like after the restart moves the counts by exactly one each way.

BAR-404.statement: A restart, crash, or process replacement during a write leaves the durable data consistent: after recovery each interrupted operation — posting a Chirp, following, deleting an account that has Chirps, Follows, and Likes — is observably either fully applied or fully absent, with no half-applied state (a Chirp with no resolvable author, a half-deleted Account with dangling references, a count out of step with its edges).

BAR-405.statement: An upgrade performed in production that changes how the data is shaped preserves the user data that existed before it: afterward the Accounts, Chirps, Follows, and Likes created before the upgrade are all present and their references still resolve, with none lost or corrupted by the upgrade.

BAR-406.statement: While an account exists, its data — the Account and profile, its Chirps, its Follows, its Likes — remains present and complete over a sustained operating period with ordinary restarts and redeploys, without the holder re-creating it. Any age-out the product applies to a live account's content is found stated in the retention posture, not met as an unexplained loss.

BAR-407.statement: When an account is deleted, the stated deletion outcome holds immediately (the account cannot sign in and no dangling reference remains), and after the product's stated, bounded retention window the deleted account's data is no longer present in the live durable store. The observed behaviour matches the stated window.

BAR-408.statement: The product states a maximum backup-retention bound that limits how long a deleted account's data can remain recoverable in backups, and that bound is consistent with the deleted-account retention posture; no backup older than the bound is retained, so deleted-account data cannot be recovered from backups indefinitely.

BAR-409.statement: An active Session survives a restart or redeploy — a request carrying its token is still accepted as the same account afterward — while a Session that has ended (sign-out) or passed its lifetime is refused after a restart and after a restore from a backup taken while it was active, never revived.

BAR-410.statement: The account's Credential and Verified contact are retained durably — a person can still sign in and the recovery path still recognises the contact after a restart and a restore — never appear in any public response, and are no longer retained in the live durable store once the account is deleted and its retention window elapses.

BAR-411.statement: For a signed-in account with Chirps and Follows, the data the product retains and the data a self-service export yields are the same set — the account's profile, its complete Chirps, and its complete followed Accounts — matching the committed durable state. No retained category of a person's own data is missing from what they can export.

BAR-412.statement: The product's data-retention and deletion posture is published where a user and an operator can find it, and it names what is retained, the live-account retention, the deleted-account retention window, the backup-retention bound, and session and private-identity-data handling. The stated posture matches the behaviour the retention and deletion criteria verify; a discrepancy is a defect.

BAR-420.statement: An operated deployment with user data produces a backup of its durable data (Accounts, Chirps, Follows, Likes) on the product's stated, regular cadence without an operator remembering to take it, and each produced backup is recorded where an operator can see it was taken. Observed over several cadence intervals, a backup appears each interval, not ad hoc.

BAR-421.statement: Backups are kept for the product's stated, bounded retention period and no longer: a backup within the period is available to restore from, a backup older than the period is no longer retained, and the period is consistent with the deleted-account backup bound (BAR-408). The oldest available backup is no older than the stated period.

BAR-422.statement: A backup taken while the product is serving restores to a state in which the model's invariants hold — every reference resolves, ids are unchanged and unreused, counts equal their edges — with no partially captured write visible. A backup that restores to an invariant-violating state is treated as unusable, not accepted.

BAR-423.statement: Backups are held so that losing the primary durable store does not also lose them: the two do not share a single point of failure, and with the primary store made unavailable a retained backup is still reachable to restore from.

BAR-424.statement: The product states a recovery-point objective — a bounded quantity of recent durable data a recovery may lose, no tighter than the backup cadence can achieve — and a recovery-time objective — a bounded duration the product may be unavailable during recovery, consistent with its availability commitment. Both name a bounded figure, not "none" without a mechanism to achieve it.

BAR-425.statement: The restore procedure is written down and followable by an operator who did not build the system: following it, that operator restores a deployment from a retained backup and returns it to service without knowledge that is not in the procedure, and the procedure names what is restored (Accounts, Chirps, Follows, Likes) and how the product is returned to serving.

BAR-426.statement: A restore from a retained backup returns the Accounts, Chirps, Follows, and Likes present at the backup point intact and consistent — references resolve, ids are unchanged and unreused, counts equal their edges, and an account deleted before the backup stays deleted with no dangling reference. A failing invariant is reported as an unsuccessful restore, never silently accepted.

BAR-427.statement: A timed restore from a backup on a representative deployment recovers the product within the stated recovery-time objective and loses no more than the stated recovery-point objective, both measured rather than asserted. A drill that exceeds either objective is reported as a defect in the objective or the procedure, not ignored.

BAR-428.statement: A deploy can be rolled back to the last working version as a routine operator operation with no user-data loss: after the rollback the product serves on the prior version and every Account, Chirp, Follow, and Like that existed before the deploy is present and unchanged, with no manual reconstruction.

BAR-429.statement: A deploy that damages or loses durable data can be recovered from by restoring from a pre-deploy backup following the restore procedure, returning the durable data to an intact and consistent state (as BAR-426) within the stated objectives. The product does not depend on the damaging deploy being reversible in place.

BAR-430.statement: A restore from a recent backup is exercised on the product's stated recurring drill cadence against a store where its correctness can be checked; the drill verifies the restored data's invariants and timing, and a failed drill is recorded and acted on rather than passed over. The drill is recurring, not a one-time pre-release event.

BAR-431.statement: A scheduled backup that fails or does not run is surfaced to operators as a visible failure state or alert, not absorbed silently, so a deployment cannot drift into having no recent usable backup unnoticed. A run of successful backups and a failed backup are distinguishable to an operator.

BAR-432.statement: The product's backup-and-recovery posture is published where an operator can find it, naming the backup cadence and retention, the recovery-point and recovery-time objectives, and the restore and rollback procedures; the stated posture matches the behaviour the backup-and-recovery criteria verify. A discrepancy is a defect.

BAR-440.statement: The product bounds the request rate it accepts from a single client, applied on both the authenticated surface and the unauthenticated surface (landing, sign-up, sign-in) and identified by client rather than only by account. A client issuing requests far faster than a person would is refused or slowed past a point — and cannot escape the bound by not signing in — while other clients continue to be served normally.

BAR-441.statement: State-creating actions — posting a Chirp, following, liking — are held to their own, tighter rate limit than reads: performing one repeatedly far faster than a person would is refused or throttled past a point, while reading remains possible within its own limit meanwhile.

BAR-442.statement: The volume of content one account can create over a longer rolling window is bounded: creating content continuously at or just under the per-action rate limit for a sustained period is eventually bounded for that window rather than accumulating without limit, and resumes in a later window.

BAR-443.statement: A request whose body is far larger than any valid chirp or form submission (for example a multi-megabyte body to a write endpoint) is refused with an error before the body is processed, while a normal, within-bounds request to the same endpoint succeeds.

BAR-444.statement: Every endpoint that returns a list serves at most the server's maximum page size: a request with no page size and a request with a page size well above the maximum both return at most the maximum number of items, with a continuation cursor when more remain, rather than the full result set.

BAR-445.statement: Exceeding any limit above refuses or throttles the excess rather than serving it, and returns a typed, machine-readable error whose category identifies it as a limit being hit — distinct from a validation error or a not-found — so a caller can tell it was limited and back off. The error is the typed contract category, not an ad-hoc string.

BAR-460.statement: The product exposes a readiness signal, distinct from liveness, whose meaning is that it can serve users: it reports ready when the durable store is reachable and the product can serve, reports not-ready when the store is unreachable from the serving process, carries a machine-distinguishable ready/not-ready indication an orchestrator can branch on without reading prose, and returns to ready on its own — without a restart or redeploy — once the condition that made it not-ready clears.

BAR-461.statement: The liveness signal reports the serving process's own health only: with the durable store unreachable but the process otherwise healthy, liveness reports alive while readiness reports not-ready, so an orchestrator restarts a genuinely crashed process but does not kill one that is alive and waiting on its store. Liveness reports not-alive only when the process itself cannot make progress.

BAR-462.statement: The health/readiness endpoint responds when queried with no account or session, and its response carries no credential, session token, verified-contact value, or other private account data, and no secret such as a connection string — it conveys serving status, not the contents of the system.

BAR-463.statement: The product records its operational events as structured, machine-parseable records with consistent, named fields (such as timestamp, severity, event category, and outcome) that a log tool can parse and filter, not as free-form prose.

BAR-464.statement: The product's logs cover the operational events needed to explain operation and failure: request handling and its outcome, errors and failures with a cause category, process start and stop, changes in durable-store connectivity, and successful and failed authentication outcomes. Provoking each in a running product produces a distinct, categorized log event with enough context to tell what happened.

BAR-465.statement: No credential, session token, verified-contact value, or other private account data appears in the product's logs or its audit trail, in any field at any severity: exercising sign-up, sign-in, recovery, session use, and representative administrative actions and then inspecting the logs and audit entries shows accounts referenced by non-secret identifier only, with no private data or secret present.

BAR-466.statement: The product exposes serving metrics that report the rate of requests handled and the rate failing, broken down enough to see which class of surface is affected (for example reads versus writes, or by outcome category); the metric labels carry no handle-linked private data, credential, or contact value.

BAR-467.statement: The product exposes a serving/availability signal that makes "the product is not serving its core loop" an observable fact: put into a degraded state in which the core loop does not work for users, the signal reflects the degradation; returned to serving, it reflects recovery. The signal is suitable to drive automated detection.

BAR-468.statement: Every action taken through the supported administrative surface — assisting a user's recovery, removing content, disabling or actioning an account — produces an audit entry naming the acting operator identity, the action taken, the target account or content, and the time. An administrative action that reaches accounts or content leaves no untraced path.

BAR-480.statement: A serving degradation — the product not serving its core loop, or serving it with elevated errors — is detected from the observability signals (the serving/availability signal, request- and error-rate metrics, saturation/headroom, durable-store interaction health) and raises a notification to the responsible operator within a bounded time, without a user having to report it first. Each alerting condition names an observability signal and a threshold or state on it; returning the product to serving raises no further alert for that incident.

BAR-481.statement: There is a stated role accountable for acknowledging and acting on a detected incident, so a fired alert has an owner; a detected major incident has a defined responder and no detected incident is left with no one responsible for it.

BAR-482.statement: When the product is unavailable or degraded, a person consulting a status surface or in-product notice sees that chirp itself is affected rather than being left to infer it from a failed action or a spinner; when the product is serving normally, the surface shows normal operation.

BAR-483.statement: The surface users consult to learn of an outage is reachable when the serving product and its durable store are fully offline: with the product taken fully down, the status surface is still reachable and reports the product as unavailable. Its availability does not require the product's serving path, store, or process to be up.

BAR-484.statement: Nothing published on the status surface, in an in-product outage notice, or in a maintenance announcement contains private account data or secret material — no credential, session token, verified-contact value, connection string, or raw internal error detail that discloses them. Inspected for a representative outage and a maintenance notice, the content describes product status in the terms a user needs and nothing more.

BAR-485.statement: With the durable store made unreachable while the serving process stays up, a user exercising the core loop meets the explained degraded or error experience the experience design specifies — an explained error, a preserved in-progress draft, a routed-to-sign-in on an expired session — not a blank page or a crashed process.

BAR-486.statement: The product states an availability target that defines what "reasonably available" means for it — a specific figure over a stated window (for example a monthly serving-availability target), proportionate to a small hosted service rather than an enterprise commitment — written down, not left implicit.

BAR-487.statement: Availability is computed in production from the serving/availability signal over the stated window, counting the product as unavailable when the signal shows it not serving its core loop, so whether the target was met is a measured fact rather than a claim. Over a window that includes at least one serving interruption, the measured result reflects the interruption and can be compared against the stated target.
